content: Croup is an acute viral respiratory infection that leads to inflammation of the upper airway mucosa, potentially causing respiratory distress. While most cases are mild, moderate to severe cases often require treatment with corticosteroids, which have a delayed onset of action, and nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline), which provides short-term relief but can cause dose-dependent side effects such as tachycardia, arrhythmias, and hypertension. In rare cases, croup can progress to respiratory failure, necessitating emergency intubation and mechanical ventilation. Heliox, a mixture of helium and oxygen, has been proposed as a therapeutic option due to its ability to reduce the viscosity of inhaled air, potentially improving airflow and reducing respiratory effort. It is currently used in emergency transport for children with severe croup, and anecdotal evidence suggests it may alleviate respiratory distress. This review updates prior versions published in 2010, 2013, and 2018. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of heliox compared to oxygen, other active treatments, placebo, or no treatment in relieving croup symptoms in children, as measured by croup scores, hospital admission rates, and intubation rates. The search for relevant studies was conducted on April 15, 2021, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and LILACS. Additional searches were performed on the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and ClinicalTrials.gov. The British Oxygen Company, a major supplier of heliox, was also contacted. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs comparing heliox to placebo, no treatment, or other active interventions in children with croup. Three RCTs involving 91 children aged 6 months to 4 years were included. The studies were conducted in emergency departments, with two in the USA and one in Spain. Heliox was administered as a mixture of 70% helium and 30% oxygen. Two studies had a low risk of bias, while one had a high risk of bias due to its open-label design. No new trials were identified for this 2021 update. In one study of 15 children with mild croup, heliox was compared to 30% humidified oxygen, both administered for 20 minutes. There was no significant difference in croup score changes between the groups at 20 minutes (mean difference [MD] −0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] −2.36 to 0.70). Similarly, there was no significant difference in mean respiratory rate (MD 6.40, 95% CI −1.38 to 14.18) or mean heart rate (MD 14.50, 95% CI −8.49 to 37.49) at 20 minutes. The evidence for these outcomes was of low certainty due to serious imprecision. All children were discharged, but data on hospitalizations, intubations, or re-presentations to emergency departments were not reported. In another study involving 47 children with moderate croup, participants received a single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.3 mg/kg) and were randomized to receive either heliox for 60 minutes or no additional treatment. Heliox may have slightly improved Taussig croup scores at 60 minutes post-intervention (MD −1.10, 95% CI −1.96 to −0.24), but there was no significant difference at 120 minutes (MD −0.70, 95% CI −1.56 to 0.16). Children treated with heliox may have had lower mean respiratory rates at 60 minutes (MD −4.94, 95% CI −9.66 to −0.22), but no significant difference was observed at 120 minutes (MD −3.17, 95% CI −7.83 to 1.49). Hospitalization rates may have differed between groups (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.04 to 5.41). The evidence for these outcomes was of low certainty, downgraded due to imprecision and the high risk of bias associated with the open-label design. Data on heart rate and intubation were not reported. In the third study, 29 children with moderate to severe croup received continuous cool mist and intramuscular dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg). They were then randomized to receive either heliox (70% helium and 30% oxygen) with one to two doses of nebulized saline or 100% oxygen with nebulized epinephrine. Gas therapy was administered continuously for three hours. Heliox may have slightly improved croup scores at 90 minutes post-intervention, but overall, there was little to no difference in outcomes based on repeated-measures analysis. The evidence for these outcomes was of low certainty, downgraded due to high risk of bias and inadequate reporting. Data on hospitalizations or re-presentations to emergency departments were not reported. None of the included studies reported on adverse events, intensive care admissions, or parental anxiety. The data could not be pooled for statistical analysis because each comparison was based on a single study. In conclusion, the available evidence is very limited, and uncertainty remains regarding the effectiveness and safety of heliox in treating croup. Heliox may not be more effective than 30% humidified oxygen for children with mild croup but may provide short-term benefits for children with moderate croup treated with dexamethasone. Its effects may be comparable to 100% oxygen combined with one or two doses of nebulized epinephrine. Adverse events were not reported, and it is unclear whether they were monitored in the included studies. Further adequately powered RCTs are needed to clarify the role of heliox in managing moderate to severe croup in children.
